questions.question: Cystic fibrosis is caused by a recessive allele of an autosomal gene. Two parents who are both carriers of the allele have a child. What is the probability that the child is a female carrier? A 1/8 B 1/4 C 1/2 D 3/4
steps: Both parents are Cc, so a child is CC (1/4), Cc (1/2) or cc (1/4); the probability of being a carrier is 1/2.
The probability that the child is female is 1/2, so 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/4.
C forgets to include the sex of the child, D is the probability that the child does not have cystic fibrosis, and A is 1/2 x 1/4.

questions.question: In shorthorn cattle, the alleles for red coat (C^R) and white coat (C^W) are codominant, and a heterozygous animal has a roan coat. A roan cow is mated with a white bull. What is the probability that the calf is roan? A 0 B 1/4 C 1/2 D 3/4
steps: The roan cow is C^R C^W and the white bull is C^W C^W.
The cow makes gametes C^R and C^W in equal numbers; the bull can only pass on C^W.
So half the calves are C^R C^W (roan) and half are C^W C^W (white): probability of roan = 1/2.
A, B and D do not follow from these gametes; B (1/4) and D (3/4) are the sort of values found in a 1 : 2 : 1 or a 3 : 1 ratio from a cross between two heterozygotes.

questions.question: A man with blood group A and a woman with blood group B have a child with blood group O. The ABO gene has three alleles: I^A and I^B, which are codominant, and I^O, which is recessive. Explain how it is possible for this child to have blood group O, and determine the probability that the next child of this couple has blood group AB.
questions.answer: Man I^A I^O and woman I^B I^O, so each passed on I^O to the O child; the probability that the next child is AB is 1/4.
steps: The child is blood group O so must be I^O I^O: each parent passed on an I^O allele.
The man is I^A I^O and the woman is I^B I^O (both heterozygous), because the I^O allele is recessive and is masked in the parents.
Gametes: man I^A or I^O, woman I^B or I^O, giving four equally likely genotypes: I^A I^B, I^A I^O, I^B I^O and I^O I^O.
Probability of blood group AB (I^A I^B) = 1/4.
accept: A genetic diagram (Punnett square) showing the cross scores as the working
25% or 0.25 for the probability
The probability is 1/4 for every child because each fertilisation is independent of the previous ones

questions.question: In cats, a gene for coat colour is on the X chromosome. The allele X^O codes for orange fur and the allele X^B codes for black fur. These two alleles are codominant. Cats with patches of orange and black fur (tortoiseshell) are almost always female. Explain why.
questions.answer: A tortoiseshell cat needs both X^O and X^B, so it needs two X chromosomes; females are XX but males are XY.
steps: The gene is on the X chromosome, so a tortoiseshell cat must be heterozygous (X^O X^B), with both codominant alleles expressed.
Females have two X chromosomes (XX), so they can carry one of each allele.
Males (XY) have only one X chromosome, so only one allele of the gene; they are orange or black, not both.
accept: Both alleles are expressed because they are codominant, so the cat shows both colours
A rare XXY male could be tortoiseshell
Males can only be X^O Y or X^B Y

questions.question: Two heterozygous tall pea plants (Tt x Tt) were crossed. The offspring were 131 tall plants and 69 dwarf plants (200 in total). A student used a chi-squared test to find out whether the results fit the expected ratio of 3 tall : 1 dwarf. The formula is chi-squared = sum of (O - E)^2 / E. The critical value at p = 0.05 with 1 degree of freedom is 3.84. Calculate the value of chi-squared and state what the student should conclude.
questions.answer: chi-squared = 9.63, which is greater than 3.84, so reject the null hypothesis: the difference from a 3:1 ratio is significant and not due to chance alone.
steps: Expected numbers: tall = 3/4 x 200 = 150; dwarf = 1/4 x 200 = 50.
9.63 is greater than the critical value of 3.84 (1 degree of freedom, p = 0.05).
So the null hypothesis is rejected: the difference from a 3:1 ratio is significant and is unlikely to be due to chance alone.

questions.question: Albinism in humans is an autosomal recessive condition. It is caused by the recessive allele (a) of a gene; the dominant allele (A) allows normal pigment to be made. Two parents with normal pigmentation have a child with albinism. Explain how this is possible.
questions.answer: Both parents are carriers (Aa); each passed on the recessive allele a, so the child is aa.
steps: Both parents must be heterozygous (Aa): the dominant allele A masks the recessive allele a in their phenotype.
Each parent passed on a recessive allele a to the child, so the child is aa and has albinism.
accept: The parents are carriers of the recessive allele
The probability of an aa child from Aa x Aa is 1/4
The recessive allele is expressed only when no dominant allele is present

questions.question: Albinism in humans is an autosomal recessive condition. It is caused by the recessive allele (a) of a gene; the dominant allele (A) allows normal pigment to be made. Two parents who are both Aa have a second child. Given that this child has normal pigmentation, calculate the probability that the child is a carrier of the allele for albinism. Show your working.
steps: Aa x Aa gives AA, Aa, Aa and aa (1 : 2 : 1).
The child has normal pigmentation, so aa is excluded: three equally likely genotypes remain (AA, Aa, Aa).
Two of these three are carriers, so the probability is 2/3.

questions.question: Albinism in humans is an autosomal recessive condition. It is caused by the recessive allele (a) of a gene; the dominant allele (A) allows normal pigment to be made. A woman with normal pigmentation has a probability of 2/3 of being a carrier (Aa). She has a child with a man who has albinism. Calculate the probability that their child has albinism.
steps: The man has albinism, so he is aa and can only pass on a.
If the woman is Aa (probability 2/3), the probability of an aa child is 1/2; if she is AA (probability 1/3), the child cannot be aa.
Probability = 2/3 x 1/2 = 1/3.

questions.question: Which mutation is most likely to cause a frameshift in the coding sequence of a gene? A insertion of a single base B substitution of a single base C substitution of a base that changes a codon into another codon for the same amino acid D deletion of three consecutive bases that make up exactly one codon
questions.answer: A: insertion of a single base
steps: Inserting one base shifts the reading frame by one base, so every codon after the insertion is changed.
B changes at most one codon, and C is a silent mutation because the genetic code is degenerate.
D removes one whole codon: one amino acid is lost but the codons after it stay in the same frame.

questions.question: A species has a diploid number of 12. Ignoring crossing over, how many different combinations of chromosomes are possible in the gametes as a result of independent assortment? A 12 B 36 C 64 D 4096
steps: A diploid number of 12 means 6 pairs of homologous chromosomes.
Number of combinations = 2^n = 2^6 = 64.
A is the diploid number, B is 6^2 and D is 2^12.

questions.question: A population of lizards lived on pale sand. A random mutation produced an allele for dark skin. The area was later covered by dark volcanic ash. Explain how natural selection could increase the frequency of the dark skin allele in the population.
questions.answer: The dark allele arose by mutation; dark lizards were better camouflaged on the ash, survived and bred more, so the allele frequency increased.
steps: The mutation produced a new allele, so there was variation: some lizards were dark and some were pale.
On the dark ash, dark lizards were better camouflaged.
Dark lizards were less likely to be eaten by predators (predation is the selection pressure), so more of them survived to breeding age.
The surviving dark lizards reproduced and passed the dark allele on to their offspring.
Over many generations the frequency of the dark allele increased and the frequency of the pale allele decreased.
accept: Pale lizards were more visible on the ash and were eaten more often
Dark lizards had a selective advantage
The dark allele frequency in the gene pool increased
More offspring are produced than survive, so there is competition for survival

questions.question: In a human population, 1 in 1600 people has an autosomal recessive condition. Use the Hardy-Weinberg equations p + q = 1 and p^2 + 2pq + q^2 = 1 to calculate the frequency of carriers of the recessive allele in the population, and the expected number of carriers in a town of 25 000 people.
questions.answer: Carrier frequency 2pq = 0.049 (4.9%); about 1200 carriers (1219) in the town.
steps: Frequency of carriers = 2pq = 2 x 0.975 x 0.025 = 0.04875, which is 0.049 (2 significant figures).
Expected number of carriers = 0.04875 x 25 000 = 1219, so about 1200.

questions.question: Distinguish between continuous variation and discontinuous variation, giving one example of each.
questions.answer: Continuous: a range of values, polygenic and environmental (e.g. height); discontinuous: distinct categories, one or few genes (e.g. ABO blood group).
steps: Continuous variation: the characteristic shows a range of values between two extremes, with no distinct categories.
Continuous variation is controlled by many genes (polygenic) and influenced by the environment; example: height (or mass, or leaf length).
Discontinuous variation: the characteristic falls into distinct categories with no intermediates.
Discontinuous variation is controlled by one or a few genes and is little affected by the environment; example: ABO blood group (or flower colour in pea plants).
accept: Continuous variation gives a normal distribution (bell-shaped curve)
Discontinuous variation is shown on a bar chart
Other examples: skin colour or seed mass (continuous); seed shape in peas (discontinuous)

questions.question: A human body cell has 46 chromosomes. Ignoring crossing over, calculate the number of genetically different gametes that one person can produce by independent assortment, and the number of genetically different zygotes that could be formed from the gametes of one particular couple by random fertilisation. Give your answers in standard form to 2 significant figures.
questions.answer: Gametes: 8.4 x 10^6; zygotes: 7.0 x 10^13.
steps: 46 chromosomes is 23 pairs, so the number of possible gametes = 2^23 = 8 388 608 = 8.4 x 10^6.
Each parent can make 2^23 different gametes, so the number of different zygotes = 2^23 x 2^23 = 2^46.

questions.question: Sickle cell anaemia is caused by a mutation in the gene for the beta-globin polypeptide of haemoglobin. In the mutated allele (Hb^S), the DNA triplet CTC on the template strand has changed to CAC. As a result the mRNA codon GAG, which codes for glutamic acid, has become GUG, which codes for valine. Name the type of gene mutation that has occurred.
questions.answer: Substitution (a point mutation).
steps: Substitution (one base replaced by another).
accept: Point mutation
Missense mutation

questions.question: Sickle cell anaemia is caused by a mutation in the gene for the beta-globin polypeptide of haemoglobin. In the mutated allele (Hb^S), the DNA triplet CTC on the template strand has changed to CAC. As a result the mRNA codon GAG, which codes for glutamic acid, has become GUG, which codes for valine. Explain how this mutation results in haemoglobin that is less able to carry oxygen.
questions.answer: Glutamic acid is replaced by valine, changing the tertiary structure; Hb^S molecules stick together at low oxygen concentration and distort the red blood cell.
steps: One amino acid in the primary structure changes: glutamic acid (charged R group) is replaced by valine (non-polar R group).
The different R group changes the bonds and interactions between R groups, so the tertiary structure (shape) of the haemoglobin changes.
At low oxygen concentration the abnormal haemoglobin molecules stick together and form fibres, which distort the red blood cell into a sickle shape so that it carries less oxygen.
accept: Sickle cells block capillaries, so less oxygen reaches the tissues
Sickle cells have a shorter lifespan, so there are fewer red blood cells (anaemia)
The haemoglobin cannot be packed into the red blood cell in the normal way

questions.question: The Hb^S allele is common in regions where malaria is common. People who are heterozygous (Hb^A Hb^S) are more resistant to malaria than people who are Hb^A Hb^A, and people who are Hb^S Hb^S often die young. Explain why the frequency of the Hb^S allele remains high in these regions.
questions.answer: Heterozygotes are more resistant to malaria, so they survive and reproduce and pass on the Hb^S allele, balancing its loss from Hb^S Hb^S individuals.
steps: Heterozygous people (Hb^A Hb^S) are more resistant to malaria, so they have a selective advantage where malaria occurs.
They are more likely to survive to reproductive age and reproduce than Hb^A Hb^A people.
They pass on the Hb^S allele to their offspring.
Hb^S Hb^S individuals are at a disadvantage, but the heterozygote advantage keeps the frequency of the Hb^S allele high.
accept: Hb^A Hb^A people are more likely to die of malaria, so the Hb^A allele is also kept in the population
Malaria is the selection pressure
Heterozygote advantage maintains both alleles (a balanced polymorphism)
In regions without malaria the Hb^S allele would decrease in frequency

questions.question: The base sequence of part of the template strand of a gene is TAC CGT AAG. What is the base sequence of the mRNA transcribed from this part of the gene? A TAC CGT AAG B UAC CGU AAG C ATG GCA TTC D AUG GCA UUC
questions.answer: D: AUG GCA UUC
steps: RNA polymerase makes mRNA complementary to the template strand: T pairs with A, A with U, C with G and G with C.
TAC CGT AAG becomes AUG GCA UUC.
A copies the template strand; B copies it with uracil in place of thymine; C is the coding (non-template) DNA strand and contains thymine, which RNA does not.

questions.question: Which row correctly shows the effect of DNA methylation and the effect of histone acetylation on the transcription of a gene? A DNA methylation decreases transcription; histone acetylation increases transcription. B DNA methylation increases transcription; histone acetylation decreases transcription. C DNA methylation decreases transcription; histone acetylation decreases transcription. D DNA methylation increases transcription; histone acetylation increases transcription.
questions.answer: A: DNA methylation decreases transcription; histone acetylation increases transcription.
steps: Methylation of cytosine bases in the promoter region prevents transcription factors and RNA polymerase binding, so it decreases (silences) transcription.
Acetylation of histones makes the chromatin less condensed, so RNA polymerase and transcription factors can reach the DNA and transcription increases.
B reverses the two effects; C and D assume that the two processes have the same effect.

questions.question: Explain how a transcription factor can increase the rate of transcription of a gene.
questions.answer: The transcription factor binds to the promoter and helps RNA polymerase to bind, so more mRNA is made.
steps: A transcription factor is a protein with a shape complementary to a specific base sequence in the promoter (regulatory) region of the gene, so it binds there.
Binding helps RNA polymerase to attach to the promoter and start transcription.
More RNA polymerase binds, so more mRNA is transcribed (and more protein is made).
accept: Binding of the transcription factor helps to position RNA polymerase on the DNA
The transcription factor may need to be activated by a signal molecule before it can bind
Transcription factors may bind to other regulatory regions of the DNA as well as the promoter

questions.question: Describe how a polypeptide is made from mRNA at a ribosome.
questions.answer: mRNA binds to a ribosome at the start codon; tRNAs bring amino acids by anticodon-codon pairing; peptide bonds join them until a stop codon.
steps: The mRNA binds to the small subunit of a ribosome at the start codon (AUG).
A tRNA carrying the specific amino acid binds to the codon by complementary base pairing between its anticodon and the codon.
The ribosome holds two tRNA molecules at a time, and a peptide bond forms between their amino acids (condensation).
The ribosome moves along the mRNA one codon at a time and the tRNA that has released its amino acid leaves.
This continues until a stop codon is reached, when the polypeptide is released.
accept: ATP (or GTP) supplies the energy for translation
Several ribosomes can translate the same mRNA at once (a polysome)
The order of the codons determines the order of the amino acids in the polypeptide
The released tRNA can pick up another amino acid

questions.question: The pre-mRNA transcribed from a gene contains 2985 nucleotides, of which 1260 nucleotides are in introns. The mature mRNA consists only of nucleotides from exons, has no untranslated regions, begins with the start codon AUG and ends with a single stop codon. Calculate the number of amino acids in the polypeptide coded for by this mRNA.
questions.answer: 574 amino acids
steps: Introns are removed by splicing: 2985 - 1260 = 1725 nucleotides remain in the mature mRNA.
Each codon has 3 nucleotides: 1725 / 3 = 575 codons.
One codon is the stop codon, which does not code for an amino acid: 575 - 1 = 574 amino acids.

questions.question: A human gene consists of four exons separated by three introns. Cells in the pancreas and cells in the liver both contain this gene, but the two cell types make different mature mRNA molecules from it. Describe how pre-mRNA is made from the gene during transcription.
questions.answer: The DNA strands separate; RNA polymerase moves along the template strand joining complementary RNA nucleotides to make pre-mRNA.
steps: The two DNA strands separate (hydrogen bonds between the bases break) at the gene, and one strand acts as the template.
RNA polymerase moves along the template strand, and free RNA nucleotides pair with the exposed bases by complementary base pairing (A with U, C with G).
RNA polymerase joins the nucleotides by phosphodiester bonds to make a pre-mRNA strand.
accept: Transcription starts at the promoter and stops at a terminator sequence
The pre-mRNA has the same base sequence as the coding strand, with uracil in place of thymine
The DNA strands rewind behind the RNA polymerase

questions.question: A human gene consists of four exons separated by three introns. Cells in the pancreas and cells in the liver both contain this gene, but the two cell types make different mature mRNA molecules from it. Explain how the two cell types can make different proteins from this one gene.
questions.answer: Alternative splicing: different combinations of exons are joined after introns are removed, giving different mature mRNAs and proteins.
steps: The pre-mRNA contains introns and exons; the introns are removed and the exons joined (splicing) in the nucleus.
In the two cell types different combinations of exons are joined (alternative splicing), so the mature mRNA molecules have different base sequences.
The different mRNA molecules are translated into polypeptides with different amino acid sequences, so different proteins are made.
accept: Different transcription factors in each cell type control which exons are kept
One gene can code for more than one protein
All body cells contain the same genes (the same DNA)

questions.question: In liver cells, methylation of cytosine bases increases in the promoter region of a gene. Explain the effect of this change on the amount of protein made from the gene.
questions.answer: Methylation of the promoter stops transcription factors and RNA polymerase binding, so less mRNA and less protein is made.
steps: Methyl groups are added to cytosine bases in the promoter region of the gene.
This stops transcription factors and RNA polymerase binding to the promoter (or makes the chromatin more condensed), so transcription decreases.
Less mRNA is made, so less protein is made by translation (the gene is silenced).
accept: Methylation is an epigenetic change that does not alter the base sequence of the DNA
The methylation pattern can be passed to daughter cells when the cell divides
Histone modification (for example removal of acetyl groups) may also condense the chromatin

questions.question: DNA fragments are separated by gel electrophoresis. Which row correctly describes the charge on the fragments, the direction they move and which fragments move furthest in a given time? A positive charge; move towards the cathode; smallest fragments move furthest. B negative charge; move towards the anode; smallest fragments move furthest. C negative charge; move towards the cathode; largest fragments move furthest. D positive charge; move towards the anode; largest fragments move furthest.
questions.answer: B: negative charge; move towards the anode; smallest fragments move furthest.
steps: The phosphate groups give DNA fragments a negative charge, so they move towards the positive electrode (the anode).
Smaller fragments move through the pores of the gel more easily, so they travel further in a given time.
A, C and D each get at least one of the charge, the direction or the effect of fragment size wrong.

questions.question: A linear DNA molecule has three recognition sites for a particular restriction endonuclease. The DNA is incubated with the enzyme until it has been cut at every recognition site. How many fragments of DNA are produced? A 3 B 4 C 5 D 6
steps: Each cut across a linear molecule produces one extra piece.
Three cuts therefore produce 3 + 1 = 4 fragments.
A confuses the number of sites with the number of fragments; C and D have no basis in the number of cuts.

questions.question: Describe how a human gene can be inserted into a bacterial plasmid, and how bacteria that have taken up the recombinant plasmid can be identified.
questions.answer: Cut gene and plasmid with the same restriction endonuclease, join with DNA ligase, insert into bacteria and identify them using a marker gene.
steps: The gene is cut from human DNA using a restriction endonuclease.
The same enzyme is used to cut the plasmid, so both have complementary sticky ends.
The sticky ends pair by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases and DNA ligase joins the sugar-phosphate backbones (phosphodiester bonds) to make the recombinant plasmid.
The recombinant plasmids are taken up by bacteria (for example after heat shock or treatment with calcium ions).
A marker gene on the plasmid (for example antibiotic resistance or a fluorescent protein) identifies the bacteria that have taken up the plasmid: they grow on antibiotic or fluoresce.
accept: The gene can be made from mRNA using reverse transcriptase (cDNA)
Insertional inactivation of a marker gene can be used to identify recombinant plasmids
A promoter must be present next to the gene so that it is expressed in the bacteria
Bacteria without the plasmid are killed by the antibiotic

questions.question: Gene therapy has been trialled for cystic fibrosis, in which a functional allele of the CFTR gene is delivered to the epithelial cells of the lungs. Describe how a functional allele could be delivered to these cells and explain why the treatment needs to be repeated.
questions.answer: The functional allele is carried in a vector (modified virus or liposome) as an aerosol into lung epithelial cells; the treatment is repeated because the cells are replaced by cells without the allele.
steps: The functional CFTR allele is inserted into a vector, such as a modified virus (disease-causing genes removed) or a liposome.
The vector is delivered to the lungs, for example in an aerosol or inhaler, where it enters the epithelial cells.
The allele is transcribed and translated in these cells so that functional CFTR protein is made.
Epithelial cells have a short life and are replaced by cell division from cells that do not contain the new allele, so the treatment has to be repeated.
accept: The virus used may be an adenovirus
The allele is not passed on to daughter cells or to the next generation (somatic gene therapy)
The immune system may destroy the vector, making repeat treatments less effective
The allele is not incorporated into the stem cells that replace the epithelial cells

questions.question: A crop plant has been genetically modified to produce a protein that is toxic to insect pests (the Bt toxin). Discuss the benefits and the risks of growing this crop.
questions.answer: Benefits: less crop damage and less insecticide. Risks: gene flow to wild relatives, pest resistance and harm to non-target insects.
steps: Benefit: less of the crop is eaten by insect pests, so the yield is higher.
Benefit: less insecticide needs to be sprayed, which reduces cost and harm to other organisms.
Risk: pollen could transfer the gene to wild relatives (gene flow), producing weeds that resist insects.
Risk: insect pests may evolve resistance to the toxin by natural selection, and non-target insects may be harmed, reducing biodiversity.
accept: Possible risk of allergic reactions or other health effects in people who eat the crop
Farmers may have to buy new GM seed every year, which is costly
Ethical objections to genetic modification of food crops
Long-term environmental effects may not be known and need monitoring

questions.question: A forensic scientist used the polymerase chain reaction (PCR) to amplify a small sample of DNA. Each cycle of the reaction consisted of three stages at 95 C, 55 C and 72 C. Explain what happens to the DNA at each of the three stages.
questions.answer: 95 C: strands separate; 55 C: primers anneal; 72 C: Taq polymerase builds new complementary strands.
steps: At 95 C the hydrogen bonds between the two DNA strands break, so the strands separate.
At 55 C primers bind (anneal) to complementary base sequences at the ends of the target DNA on each single strand.
At 72 C Taq polymerase adds free nucleotides to the 3' end of each primer, making a new complementary strand.
accept: Primers are short single-stranded lengths of DNA
72 C is close to the optimum temperature of Taq polymerase
Nucleotides are added by complementary base pairing
The cycle is repeated so that the number of DNA copies doubles each time

questions.question: A forensic scientist used the polymerase chain reaction (PCR) to amplify a small sample of DNA. Each cycle of the reaction consisted of three stages at 95 C, 55 C and 72 C. The DNA polymerase used in PCR is Taq polymerase, from a bacterium that lives in hot springs. Explain why Taq polymerase is used rather than human DNA polymerase.
questions.answer: Taq polymerase is heat-stable, so it is not denatured at 95 C and is not needed to be added each cycle.
steps: Taq polymerase is heat-stable (thermostable): it keeps its shape and function at 95 C.
Human DNA polymerase would be denatured at 95 C, so fresh enzyme would have to be added every cycle.
accept: Taq polymerase comes from a thermophilic bacterium (Thermus aquaticus)
Taq polymerase has an optimum temperature of about 72 C
Using Taq polymerase allows the cycles to be automated

questions.question: In a PCR the number of copies of the target DNA doubles in each cycle. Each cycle takes 90 s. Starting from one molecule of the target DNA, calculate the minimum time, in minutes, needed to produce at least 1.0 x 10^6 copies.
questions.answer: 30 minutes
steps: After n cycles the number of copies is 2^n; 2^19 = 524 288 is too few but 2^20 = 1 048 576 is more than 1.0 x 10^6, so 20 cycles are needed.
1800 s / 60 = 30 minutes.
